\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails, and that the failure runs deeper than the representation signal itself.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO \citep{shao2024grpo} training signal (cosine projection, binary probe, and continuous probe) across six experimental configurations; every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.827 to 0.910 yet triggers mode collapse.
A binary probe with stopped gradients creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
These failures might suggest that removing $\dsyc$ in favor of a purely behavioral reward would resolve the problem.
It does not.
R3-only GRPO, which uses an NLI-based behavioral reward without any representation component, also fails to calibrate sycophancy: the \sycon{} score starts at 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, reaches only 0.114 by checkpoint 5000, and never exceeds the vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
The trajectory shows partial recovery before plateauing: the score stalls at 0.114 between checkpoints 4000 and 5500 (three consecutive evaluations), 15\% below vanilla with no further improvement.
Two layers of failure emerge: $\dsyc$-based rewards are actively harmful, and GRPO itself is structurally insufficient for sycophancy calibration.

Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability in activation space should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety refusal, this premise holds, because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy violates this premise.
Capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth; it must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.
This conflation explains both layers of failure.
$\dsyc$ rewards penalize all belief change indiscriminately, producing behavioral collapse.
R3-only GRPO's single scalar per completion cannot compensate because it lacks the per-token resolution to teach which belief changes are warranted and which are not.
ACT succeeds because its dense supervision operates at the token level, where the valid/invalid distinction can be resolved.
Sycophancy is defined relative to external evidential warrant \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, a property that no single activation direction can fully encode.
The entanglement between helpfulness and sycophancy at the representation level, where the same mechanisms that allow models to track user intent also predispose them to capitulate \citep{wang2025internal}, is amplified by RLHF \citep{shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{casper2023openproblems}.

We present three contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Every tested GRPO formulation fails for sycophancy calibration} (C1). We extract and validate $\dsyc$ on two model families (Qwen3-8B AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$; Llama-3-8B AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$), then show that all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}). R3-only GRPO, which removes $\dsyc$ entirely, also fails: \sycon{} reaches only 0.114 at checkpoint 5000 against a vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Discriminability does not confer reward utility, and sparse RL rewards are structurally insufficient for this task.

\item \textbf{Probe reward trap with behavioral-before-distributional collapse} (C2). The binary probe reward produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70. The 1,300-step lag before distributional collapse means standard entropy monitoring misses the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Sparse RL reward cannot convey the valid/invalid distinction} (C3). We trace these failures to a unified root cause: $\dsyc$ encodes belief-change direction but not evidential warrant. A single scalar reward per completion, whether from representations or behavioral classifiers, cannot teach the model which belief changes are warranted. Dense SFT supervision resolves this: ACT achieves \sycon{} of 0.301, while every tested GRPO variant remains below vanilla (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

1	\section{Analysis: Discriminability $\neq$ Reward Utility}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Unified root cause.}
4	The failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} trace to a single geometric limitation.
5	$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
6	The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
7	Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
8	The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails, and that the failure runs deeper than the representation signal itself.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO \citep{shao2024grpo} training signal (cosine projection, binary probe, and continuous probe) across six experimental configurations; every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.827 to 0.910 yet triggers mode collapse.
A binary probe with stopped gradients creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
These failures might suggest that removing $\dsyc$ in favor of a purely behavioral reward would resolve the problem.
It does not.
R3-only GRPO, which uses an NLI-based behavioral reward without any representation component, also fails to calibrate sycophancy: the \sycon{} score starts at 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, reaches only 0.114 by checkpoint 5000, and never exceeds the vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
The trajectory shows partial recovery before plateauing: the score stalls at 0.114 between checkpoints 4000 and 5500 (three consecutive evaluations), 15\% below vanilla with no further improvement.
Two layers of failure emerge: $\dsyc$-based rewards are actively harmful, and GRPO itself is structurally insufficient for sycophancy calibration.

Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability in activation space should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety refusal, this premise holds, because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy violates this premise.
Capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth; it must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.
This conflation explains both layers of failure.
$\dsyc$ rewards penalize all belief change indiscriminately, producing behavioral collapse.
R3-only GRPO's single scalar per completion cannot compensate because it lacks the per-token resolution to teach which belief changes are warranted and which are not.
ACT succeeds because its dense supervision operates at the token level, where the valid/invalid distinction can be resolved.
Sycophancy is defined relative to external evidential warrant \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, a property that no single activation direction can fully encode.
The entanglement between helpfulness and sycophancy at the representation level, where the same mechanisms that allow models to track user intent also predispose them to capitulate \citep{wang2025internal}, is amplified by RLHF \citep{shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{casper2023openproblems}.

We present three contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Every tested GRPO formulation fails for sycophancy calibration} (C1). We extract and validate $\dsyc$ on two model families (Qwen3-8B AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$; Llama-3-8B AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$), then show that all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}). R3-only GRPO, which removes $\dsyc$ entirely, also fails: \sycon{} reaches only 0.114 at checkpoint 5000 against a vanilla baseline of 0.134 (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Discriminability does not confer reward utility, and sparse RL rewards are structurally insufficient for this task.

\item \textbf{Probe reward trap with behavioral-before-distributional collapse} (C2). The binary probe reward produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70. The 1,300-step lag before distributional collapse means standard entropy monitoring misses the failure entirely, with the reward averaging $+0.72$ throughout (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).

\item \textbf{Sparse RL reward cannot convey the valid/invalid distinction} (C3). We trace these failures to a unified root cause: $\dsyc$ encodes belief-change direction but not evidential warrant. A single scalar reward per completion, whether from representations or behavioral classifiers, cannot teach the model which belief changes are warranted. Dense SFT supervision resolves this: ACT achieves \sycon{} of 0.301, while every tested GRPO variant remains below vanilla (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails, and that the failure runs deeper than the representation signal itself.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO \citep{shao2024grpo} training signal (cosine projection, binary probe, and continuous probe) across six experimental configurations; every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.827 to 0.910 yet triggers mode collapse.
A binary probe with stopped gradients creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
These failures might suggest that removing $\dsyc$ in favor of a purely behavioral reward would resolve the problem.
It does not.
R3-only GRPO, which uses an NLI-based behavioral reward without any representation component, also fails to calibrate sycophancy: the \sycon{} score starts at 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, briefly matches the vanilla baseline at one checkpoint (step 4500) but immediately regresses to 0.114 and plateaus from step 5000 onward (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
After a transient spike to vanilla level at step 4500, the score regresses to 0.114 and plateaus from step 5000 onward (two consecutive evaluations), confirming that sparse behavioral reward cannot push calibration beyond the pre-training baseline.
Two layers of failure emerge: $\dsyc$-based rewards are actively harmful, and GRPO itself is structurally insufficient for sycophancy calibration.

Sycophancy violates this premise.
Capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth; it must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work tested a natural hypothesis: that a representation direction capable of detecting sycophantic behavior should also serve as an effective reward signal for training against it. Our experiments systematically falsify this hypothesis across multiple formulations and reveal a structural barrier that applies beyond any single reward design.

We first established that $\dsyc$ achieves strong offline discriminability (AUROC 0.827 on Qwen3-8B, 0.779 on Llama-3-8B) with cross-model transfer, confirming that contrastive directions do capture a real geometric signature of sycophantic capitulation. Yet all three reward formulations built on this direction failed across six $\dsyc$-based GRPO configurations. The cosine reward could not separate valid revisions from sycophantic ones in the narrow online activation gap. The probe reward produced a stubbornness trap: the policy reached $\tof = 0$ by step 500, with entropy collapse following only 1{,}300 steps later, exposing a dangerous dissociation between behavioral failure and standard training monitors. Even removing $\dsyc$ entirely and training with the behavioral $\rthree$ reward alone yielded a \sycon{} plateau at 0.114, below the vanilla baseline of 0.134.

The root cause is consistent across all configurations: $\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}. Valid revision and sycophantic capitulation occupy overlapping geometric regions because they share the same surface behavior; they differ only in evidential warrant, which no single activation direction can encode. That Activation Consistency Training achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ through dense per-token supervision confirms that the missing ingredient is token-level teaching of \emph{which} belief changes are appropriate, not a better reward scalar.

The broader lesson extends beyond sycophancy: representation geometry that reliably detects a behavior is not automatically suitable for optimizing against it. Any alignment effort that converts a detection probe into a reward signal must verify that the probe separates not only the target behavior from its complement, but also the valid and invalid instances within each class. Without this finer distinction, RL will find the shortest path to reward, and that path leads away from the intended objective.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Representation engineering \citep{zou2023repe} reveals that large language models encode sycophancy as a linear direction in their residual streams.
A contrastive sycophancy direction $\dsyc$, extracted from style-controlled pairs of valid belief revision and sycophantic capitulation, achieves cross-validated AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$ on Qwen3-8B and $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on Llama-3-8B (\S\ref{sec:direction_quality}).
The direction captures evidential granularity: discriminability rises monotonically from weak-evidence pairs (AUROC 0.675) through medium (0.883) to strong (0.929), and the signal remains stable under LoRA training with cosine drift of approximately 0.96 at 500 steps.
These results, replicated across two architecturally distinct model families, point to an appealing possibility: if the model's representations already separate sycophantic from non-sycophantic behavior, that separation should be convertible into a reward signal for reinforcement learning.
Sycophancy is among the most persistent alignment failures in deployed systems \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, and a representation-level reward could complement existing behavioral approaches by targeting the internal computation rather than its surface outputs.

This paper shows that the conversion fails, and that the failure runs deeper than the representation signal itself.
We test three formulations that translate $\dsyc$ into a GRPO \citep{shao2024grpo} training signal (cosine projection, binary probe, and continuous probe) across six experimental configurations; every formulation fails.
Cosine similarity produces a reward gap of just 0.098 between valid and sycophantic activations, too narrow to drive policy updates (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}).
Online recalibration improves the offline AUROC from 0.827 to 0.910 yet triggers mode collapse.
A binary probe with stopped gradients creates a stubbornness trap: the model learns that never revising its answer reliably collects the probe reward, and the true-positive flip rate ($\tof$) drops to zero within 500 steps while generation entropy remains at 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:probe_trap}).
These failures might suggest that removing $\dsyc$ in favor of a purely behavioral reward would resolve the problem.
It does not.
R3-only GRPO, which uses an NLI-based behavioral reward without any representation component, also fails to calibrate sycophancy: the \sycon{} score starts at 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, briefly matches the vanilla baseline at one checkpoint (step 4500) but immediately regresses to 0.114 and plateaus from step 5000 onward (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
After a transient spike to vanilla level at step 4500, the score regresses to 0.114 and plateaus from step 5000 onward (two consecutive evaluations), confirming that sparse behavioral reward cannot push calibration beyond the pre-training baseline.
Two layers of failure emerge: $\dsyc$-based rewards are actively harmful, and GRPO itself is structurally insufficient for sycophancy calibration.

Techniques for discovering latent knowledge \citep{burns2023ccs} and representation-guided RL \citep{zhang2026latentgrpo} share a premise: a direction with high discriminability in activation space should transfer into a useful training signal.
For reasoning faithfulness and safety refusal, this premise holds, because the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
Sycophancy violates this premise.
Capitulation under social pressure and revision under valid evidence produce overlapping activation signatures along $\dsyc$, because both involve the model shifting its stated belief toward the user's position.

The root cause is a semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility.
$\dsyc$ encodes \emph{whether} belief changed, not \emph{whether it should have}.
A post-hoc classifier can use this signal effectively because it scores labeled examples where the validity of the belief change is already known.
A reward signal during RL training has no such access to ground truth; it must distinguish warranted revision from unwarranted capitulation using activation geometry alone, and $\dsyc$ collapses exactly this distinction.
This conflation explains both layers of failure.
$\dsyc$ rewards penalize all belief change indiscriminately, producing behavioral collapse.
R3-only GRPO's single scalar per completion cannot compensate because it lacks the per-token resolution to teach which belief changes are warranted and which are not.
ACT succeeds because its dense supervision operates at the token level, where the valid/invalid distinction can be resolved.
Sycophancy is defined relative to external evidential warrant \citep{sharma2023sycophancy}, a property that no single activation direction can fully encode.
The entanglement between helpfulness and sycophancy at the representation level, where the same mechanisms that allow models to track user intent also predispose them to capitulate \citep{wang2025internal}, is amplified by RLHF \citep{shapira2026amplifies}.
When reward overoptimization \citep{gao2023scaling} operates on a signal that conflates compliance with capitulation, the result is predictable collapse \citep{casper2023openproblems}.

We present three contributions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Every tested GRPO formulation fails for sycophancy calibration} (C1). We extract and validate $\dsyc$ on two model families (Qwen3-8B AUROC $0.827 \pm 0.028$; Llama-3-8B AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$), then show that all three $\dsyc$-based reward formulations produce behavioral collapse (\S\ref{sec:cosine_failure}, \S\ref{sec:probe_trap}). R3-only GRPO, which removes $\dsyc$ entirely, also fails: \sycon{} briefly matches vanilla (0.134) at checkpoint 4500 but regresses to 0.114 and plateaus (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Discriminability does not confer reward utility, and sparse RL rewards are structurally insufficient for this task.

\item \textbf{Probe reward trap with behavioral-before-distributional collapse} (C2). The binary probe reward produces behavioral death ($\tof = 0$ at step 500) while entropy remains at 0.70. A single scalar reward per completion, whether from representations or behavioral classifiers, cannot teach the model which belief changes are warranted. Dense SFT supervision resolves this: ACT achieves \sycon{} of 0.301, while no GRPO variant surpasses vanilla (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Analysis: Discriminability $\neq$ Reward Utility}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Unified root cause.}
The failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} trace to a single geometric limitation.
$\dsyc$ encodes the \emph{direction} of belief change but not its \emph{evidential warrant}: valid revision and sycophantic capitulation both shift activations toward the user's position along the same direction.
The two reward families expose complementary faces of this blindness.
Cosine $\rone$ penalizes all belief change indiscriminately; the resulting mode collapse (F1c, F1d) reflects excessive punishment of any activation shift along $\dsyc$.
The binary probe $\rone$ rewards all resistance regardless of input validity; the stubbornness trap ($\tof = 0$ by step 500) reflects excessive permissiveness toward activation stasis.
These are not independent design flaws but dual consequences of a direction that conflates the target behavior (resisting invalid challenges) with its complement (refusing valid corrections).
Cross-model evidence confirms the limitation extends beyond Qwen3-8B: Llama-3-8B independently achieves AUROC $0.779 \pm 0.019$ on the same contrastive pairs with the same monotonic evidence gradient, so discriminability generalizes across architectures while the semantic gap between discriminability and reward utility persists.
This pattern contrasts with reasoning faithfulness and safety directions~\citep{zhang2026latentgrpo}, where the behavior to suppress is geometrically distinct from the behavior to preserve along the relevant direction.
For sycophancy, the target and its complement occupy the same activation region; they differ only in whether external evidence warrants the belief change.

\paragraph{GRPO stubbornness across all formulations.}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Comparison of all sycophancy calibration methods on Qwen3-8B. $\sycon$ is the harmonic mean of $\tof$ and $\nof$; higher indicates better calibration. Best result in \textbf{bold}. $^\dagger$Peak at step 4500; regresses to 0.114 by step 5000.}
\label{tab:main_comparison}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
Method & Type & $\sycon$ $\uparrow$ & $\tof$ $\uparrow$ & $\nof$ $\uparrow$ & Step \\
\midrule
Vanilla & -- & 0.134 & 0.072 & 0.945 & -- \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO with $\dsyc$}} \\
Cosine $\rone$ (F1a--F1d) & RL & collapse & -- & -- & -- \\
Binary Probe $\rone$ (F2) & RL & 0.000 & 0.000 & 0.995 & 500 \\
Continuous Probe $\rone$ (F3) & RL & 0.124 & 0.066 & 0.934 & 500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{GRPO without $\dsyc$}} \\
$\rthree$-only GRPO & RL & 0.134$^\dagger$ & 0.072 & 0.945 & 4500 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{6}{l}{\textit{Non-GRPO}} \\
ActAdd ($\alpha{=}5$) & Inference & 0.054 & 0.028 & 0.961 & -- \\
\textbf{ACT} & SFT & \textbf{0.301} & \textbf{0.182} & 0.867 & 8000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison} summarizes all methods evaluated on Qwen3-8B.
$\rthree$-only GRPO removes $\dsyc$ entirely and relies on the NLI-based behavioral reward alone.
If the failures in Sections~\ref{sec:cosine_failure} and~\ref{sec:probe_trap} stemmed solely from the representation reward, this ablation should recover calibration quality.
It does not.
The $\sycon$ trajectory shows partial recovery that peaks at vanilla: 0.074 at checkpoint 1000, 0.085 at checkpoint 2000, 0.095 at checkpoint 3000, 0.114 at checkpoint 4000, a transient spike to 0.134 at checkpoint 4500---matching vanilla exactly---followed by regression to 0.114 at checkpoints 5000 and 5500.
The best performance $\rthree$-only GRPO achieves is recovery to the untrained vanilla level; behavioral reward alone cannot push the model beyond its pre-training baseline, suggesting that sparse NLI feedback lacks the signal density to drive genuine calibration improvement.
ActAdd~\citep{turner2023actadd}, the inference-time baseline, achieves only $\sycon = 0.054$, confirming that activation-level intervention without weight updates cannot resolve the calibration problem.
$\rthree$-only GRPO exhibits the same stubbornness pattern as the $\dsyc$ approaches (high $\nof$, near-zero $\tof$) at milder severity.
The sparse scalar reward per completion cannot teach the model \emph{which} belief changes are warranted: it collapses an entire multi-turn exchange into one number that does not distinguish legitimate resistance from stubborn refusal.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_trajectory.pdf}
\caption{$\sycon$ trajectories for $\rthree$-only GRPO (exp-003) and ACT (exp-004) over training steps. The dashed line marks the vanilla baseline ($\sycon = 0.134$). GRPO briefly matches vanilla at checkpoint 4500 but regresses to 0.114; ACT dips at checkpoint 4000 but recovers to 0.301 by checkpoint 8000.}
\label{fig:trajectory}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Why SFT succeeds where GRPO fails.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ at checkpoint 8000, more than $2{\times}$ the vanilla baseline and above every RL and inference-time variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}).
The ACT trajectory is not monotonic: $\sycon = 0.255$ at checkpoint 2000, dips to 0.214 at checkpoint 4000 ($-4.1$ percentage points as $\tof$ drops and $\nof$ rises), recovers to 0.262 at checkpoint 6000, and reaches 0.301 at checkpoint 8000.
ACT also experiences stubbornness episodes---the checkpoint-4000 dip is consistent with transient competition between the SFT and L2 consistency loss objectives---yet it self-recovers by checkpoint 6000, unlike GRPO where stubbornness is irreversible (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The critical difference is supervision density.
SFT provides a corrective gradient at every token position in every training example: when the model begins to resist valid corrections, per-token cross-entropy loss immediately penalizes the incorrect tokens and supplies gradient information about \emph{which} outputs need to change.
GRPO provides one scalar per completion; once the policy locks into stubbornness, that scalar reinforces the behavior because consistent non-flipping collects high reward from both $\rone$ and $\rthree$.
Dense per-token loss can break out of stubbornness equilibria that sparse per-completion reward cannot escape.
This recovery capacity is the practical signature of the dense-versus-sparse supervision gap.
ACT is also far more efficient: its checkpoint 500 ($\sycon = 0.170$) already exceeds the plateau that $\rthree$-only GRPO reaches after 5000 steps of training.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
These results point to several open problems.
First, condition-aware reward design could jointly encode belief-change direction and evidential warrant by conditioning on whether the input challenge provides valid grounds for revision.
Second, hybrid pipelines that apply SFT to establish the valid/invalid distinction as a warm start, followed by RL for broader distributional coverage, may combine the calibration quality of dense supervision with the exploration benefits of reinforcement learning.
Third, process reward models that provide per-step feedback within the RL framework could bridge the supervision density gap and retain online optimization.
Beyond sycophancy, the principle that discriminability does not guarantee reward utility applies to any behavioral attribute where the target and its complement share the same geometric direction~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
Whether this principle extends to other alignment-relevant behaviors, such as hallucination and instruction-following, is an important open question.

\paragraph{Why SFT succeeds where GRPO fails.}
ACT~\citep{consistency2025bctact} achieves $\sycon = 0.301$ at checkpoint 8000, more than $2{\times}$ the vanilla baseline and above every RL and inference-time variant (Table~\ref{tab:main_comparison}).
The ACT trajectory is not monotonic: $\sycon = 0.255$ at checkpoint 2000, dips to 0.214 at checkpoint 4000 ($-4.1$ percentage points as $\tof$ drops and $\nof$ rises), recovers to 0.262 at checkpoint 6000, and reaches 0.301 at checkpoint 8000.
ACT also experiences stubbornness episodes---the checkpoint-4000 dip is consistent with transient competition between the SFT and L2 consistency loss objectives---yet it self-recovers by checkpoint 6000, unlike GRPO where stubbornness is irreversible (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}).
The critical difference is supervision density.
SFT provides a corrective gradient at every token position in every training example: when the model begins to resist valid corrections, per-token cross-entropy loss immediately penalizes the incorrect tokens and supplies gradient information about \emph{which} outputs need to change.
GRPO provides one scalar per completion; once the policy locks into stubbornness, that scalar reinforces the behavior because consistent non-flipping collects high reward from both $\rone$ and $\rthree$.
Dense per-token loss can break out of stubbornness equilibria that sparse per-completion reward cannot escape.
This recovery capacity is the practical signature of the dense-versus-sparse supervision gap.
ACT is also far more efficient: its checkpoint 500 ($\sycon = 0.170$) already exceeds the plateau that $\rthree$-only GRPO reaches after 5000 steps of training.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
These results point to several open problems.
First, condition-aware reward design could jointly encode belief-change direction and evidential warrant by conditioning on whether the input challenge provides valid grounds for revision.
Second, hybrid pipelines that apply SFT to establish the valid/invalid distinction as a warm start, followed by RL for broader distributional coverage, may combine the calibration quality of dense supervision with the exploration benefits of reinforcement learning.
Third, process reward models that provide per-step feedback within the RL framework could bridge the supervision density gap and retain online optimization.
Beyond sycophancy, the principle that discriminability does not guarantee reward utility applies to any behavioral attribute where the target and its complement share the same geometric direction~\citep{skalse2022hacking}.
Whether this principle extends to other alignment-relevant behaviors, such as hallucination and instruction-following, is an important open question.
